match.reason: The nearest bank point, Shape of a distribution, covers symmetric and skewed shapes and the 1.5 × IQR outlier rule at a suitable Year 11 depth, but it does not teach the bell-shaped idea with most data within a few standard deviations of the mean, and the other bank points that do cover that idea are pitched at Year 12 depth.

draft.title: Shapes of distributions
card: Symmetric
The two sides of the display are roughly mirror images, with the peak near the middle.
Skewed
One side has a long tail. If the tail points to the higher values, it is positively skewed (skewed right). If it points to the lower values, it is negatively skewed (skewed left).
Bell-shaped

A symmetric distribution with one peak in the middle that tapers off evenly on both sides. About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3.
Example: test scores have a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 5. If they are bell-shaped, about 95% of scores lie within 2 standard deviations, which is from 50 to 70.
draft.remember: The tail names the skew. In a bell shape, 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.

a.q: A histogram has its peak at the low values and a long tail stretching to the high values. What is its shape?
a.why: The long tail points to the higher values, so the distribution is positively skewed. It is not negatively skewed, because that name follows the tail and not the side where the peak sits.
a.clue: Name the shape by the direction of the tail.

b.q: The heights of plants in a nursery are bell-shaped, with a mean of 40 cm and a standard deviation of 4 cm. About 68% of the plants have heights between which values?
b.why: About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, so 40 − 4 = 36 and 40 + 4 = 44. The range 32 cm to 48 cm is within 2 standard deviations, which holds about 95%.
